judge_assessment.explanation: I checked every arithmetic claim in the verdict against the artifacts and all of them hold: the cell read 30; the grand total 30+20+45+105 = 200; the difference 105−20 = 85; the row relative frequencies 100·30/50 = 60 and 100·45/150 = 30; the column relative frequencies 100·30/75 = 40 and 100·20/125 = 16; the gap 60−30 = 30 percentage points; and the median of (55,70,45,60,60) = 60. The judge's claim that 'all denominators match the requested row or column population' is exactly right and is the thing most likely to be wrong on a two-way-table sheet — problems 3 and 5 divide by the row totals 50 and 150, problems 6 and 7 by the column totals 75 and 125, and each stem names its base in words before asking. I also checked the two dominant systemic findings rather than assuming: problem 10 is the only open item and it IS declared manual with acceptance criteria, and final_response.md names the worksheet, the answer key and the study guide with page counts. The Quick Answers bank prints a real value on every row except 10, which is the genuine manual, so the relation and builtin rendering defects do not arise here. I found no defect worth a backlog item. The only thing I looked at twice — problem 1's 'Name the row and the column you used' and problems 6-7's 'state which total you divided by' — are riders that restate the base already named in the stem, and the key answers each; they carry no independent mathematical content that could be wrong while the checked value is right, so I did not file them.

strengths_to_preserve: The row totals were chosen unequal on purpose — 50 athletes against 150 non-athletes — so the raw counts 30 and 45 point the OPPOSITE way from the percentages 60 and 30. That single design decision is what makes the standard's whole point unavoidable, and problem 4 (a raw-count comparison) is deliberately placed so problem 10 can criticise it.

Problems 3/5 and 6/7 use the SAME cells with different denominators and land on different numbers (60/30 versus 40/16), so 'row relative frequency' and 'column relative frequency' become distinguishable by result rather than by vocabulary.

All three declared traps are the real confusions and were machine-checked as distinguishable: dividing by the grand total (15), and using the row total where the column total belongs (60 instead of 40, 40 instead of 16). A wrong answer on this sheet tells the grader which mistake produced it.

The final response flags an honest limitation rather than hiding it: every problem is tagged 8.SP.A.1 because references/standards-map.md has no 8.SP.A.4 row, and it says so and says which code would be more precise.
case_summary: A clean, complete two-way-table workshop and the strongest instruction-following case in this batch. One survey table with all four inner cells, both row totals, both column totals and the grand total drives ten problems that ramp from reading a cell to comparing row against column bases, and every one of the nine machine-checkable answers recomputes correctly. Problem 10 — the only open item — is declared manual with a grading note that names what a full-credit explanation must contain (the unequal row totals, not merely that 60 exceeds 30). The study guide's pet-clinic table repeats the structure at smaller scale and includes a 3-percentage-point try-it so the student also meets the 'no association' case. Five pages for ten problems, all gates green, no defect found: the 32/32 is right and I have nothing to add to it.
